Acrylic paint-along · beginner

A glowing brass lantern hanging from a snowy wooden post on a moonlit winter night, with dark pines and rolling snow behind

Start on a plain white canvas. Paint the sky first, then each part of the scene from farthest to nearest, each straight over the one behind it. Then the main subject, texture with simple brush moves, shadows, and highlights last.

19 stepsCanvas: 16 x 12 inFocal point: The lantern's bright yellow core and the warm pool of light it throws on the snow below it Light: Two lights: a cool full moon at the upper left, and the warm lantern in the middle, which lights the snow under it, the left side of the post, and the inside edges of its own brass frame. Snow tops catch the light on their upper edges.How this lesson was made

Brushes

  • 1 inch wide flat: Blend the night skyFlat: square end, for big areas and straight edges
  • #10 round: Circle in the moonRound: pointed tip, thin or thick depending on how hard you press
  • #2 round: Dot in the starsRound: pointed tip, thin or thick depending on how hard you press
  • #6 fan: Stamp the dark pinesFan: bristles spread like a fan, for grass, fur, and soft blending
  • 1 inch flat: Lay in the snow in shadow blueFlat: square end, for big areas and straight edges
  • 3/4 inch flat: Shade the hollows between driftsFlat: square end, for big areas and straight edges
  • 1/2 inch flat: Block in the post, arm and railsFlat: square end, for big areas and straight edges
  • 1/4 inch flat: Light the side facing the lanternFlat: square end, for big areas and straight edges
  • #8 round: Glow the middle of the glassRound: pointed tip, thin or thick depending on how hard you press
  • #4 round: Light the coreRound: pointed tip, thin or thick depending on how hard you press
  • #6 round: Build the brass cap and baseRound: pointed tip, thin or thick depending on how hard you press
  • #2 liner: Line the bars, ring and hookLiner: long, very thin bristles, for fine lines like twigs and grass
  • 3/4 inch old stiff flat: Scumble the warm light on the snowOld stiff flat: worn, splayed bristles, for rough texture like grass and foliage

Before you start

Placing shapes with a transfer outline optional

The transfer outline (optional)

The outlines of the main shapes, on a grid of quarters: 1 The snowy hill and drifts; 2 The wooden post, its arm and the fence rails; 3 The glowing lantern. On your 16 x 12 in canvas the grid lines are 4 in apart across and 3 in apart down. Before the stage that starts one, you can lightly chalk its outline on the canvas, measuring from the edges with a ruler.

Strokes to try on scrap paper first

Each one's card is open in the step that first uses it.

  • Side-to-side blend, first in step 1.
  • Small circles, first in step 2.
  • Dotting, first in step 3.
  • Fan brush tapping, first in step 4. Try it on scrap paper first.
  • Curved strokes, first in step 5.
  • Dry brush, first in step 6. Try it on scrap paper first: wipe the brush until it leaves broken marks.
  • Building from pieces, first in step 7.
  • Liner work, first in step 14. Try a few lines on scrap paper first.
  • Scumbling, first in step 17.

Getting started

The other basics are in the steps where they matter.

Before you start

Not checked yet

  • Two water jars: one to rinse the brush, one kept clean for thinning paint. A big clear jar shows when the rinse water is dirty.
  • A rag or paper towel, to wipe the brush between colors.
  • Put out bigger puddles of paint than you think you need. Big puddles stay wet longer than small smears.
  • Lay your colors out the same way every time, so they're easy to find and don't get dragged into each other.

Keep your colors clean

Not checked yet

  • Wipe the brush on a rag between colors.
  • Rinse it fully before going into white.
  • Rinse often. Dirty water tints every color with the last one.
  • Mix on the palette, not on the canvas. Two or three colors at most: stop when the color is right.

Keep paint from drying on the palette

Not checked yet

  • Acrylic on a brushstroke stays wet for only a few minutes.
  • Mist the palette lightly with a spray bottle now and then. Only lightly: too much water weakens the paint.
  • Cover the paint when you aren't using it.

Paint thickness and how much is on the brush

Not checked yet

  • Each step's Load line says two different things. How thick the paint is, and how much of it is on the brush. Creamy paint can be a full load or a light one.

How thick the paint is

How much is on the brush

How much water

Not checked yet

  • Keep water to about half the mix or less. More than that makes weak, see-through color that can lift when you paint over it.
  • For covering, use the paint thick, with little or no water.
  • After rinsing, wipe the metal part of the brush dry.
If something goes wrong not checked yet

Fixing a mistake

Not checked yet

  • Acrylic is forgiving. Let the area dry, then paint over it and try again.
  • Don't keep working a spot that's half dry. Leave it, work somewhere else, and come back.

The night sky 3 steps

STEP 1 OF 19 · The night sky, 1 of 3

Blend the night sky

  1. Inside the outlined area, all the way across from the top edge. Its bottom is about 5 1/2 in from the top edge.
  2. The outline also runs under where the snowy hill and drifts, and the lamplight on the snow will go: paint straight through there.
  3. Paints, top to bottom: Night blue, then Midnight blue.
  4. Brush: 1 inch wide flat. Load: Creamy paint. An even coat.
  5. Start with the darkest color and stroke side to side. Without rinsing, pick up the next color and paint under the darkest band. Then stroke back up over the join several times.
  6. It should leave smooth bands of color, with a soft join where two wet colors meet.
  7. Watch out: Blending after the paint has started to drag. Acrylic sets in minutes, and scrubbing setting paint lifts it and leaves streaks. Fix: stop as soon as it drags.
  8. Let it dry, then blend a new thin layer on top.

Tip: Carry the blue past the outline all the way to the bottom edge of the canvas, as the after picture shows. The after picture already shows the stars; leave them for step 3 and paint the sky plain.

Basics: Making a color lighter or darker

Making a color lighter or darker

Not checked yet

  • To lighten: add the color to the white a little at a time, not white to the color.
  • White also dulls a color. Too much turns it chalky.
  • To darken: add the dark into the lighter mix in small amounts.
  • For the next lighter value of something, start from the mix you already have and add white, so the colors stay related.
Basics: Colors dry darker

Colors dry darker

Not checked yet

  • Acrylic looks lighter when wet than when dry.
  • Before a big area, paint a test swatch and let it dry before judging the mix.

Stroke: Side-to-side blend how to do it, not checked yet

Side-to-side blend

Not checked yet

With. wide flat; 3/4 inch wash brush

Load. Creamy paint. An even coat.

Motion. Start with the darkest color and stroke side to side. Without rinsing, pick up the next lighter color and paint below it. Then stroke back up over the join several times.

What it leaves. Smooth bands of color, with a soft join where two wet colors meet.

Then. Stroke back over each join while it's wet.

Blend two colors side to side

Dashed outline: what to paint in that picture. Arrows: which way to move the brush.

If it goes wrong.

  • A hard line where two colors meet. Add more of the lighter color at the join and blend again.
  • Two very different colors won't blend. Mix a bridge color from the two on the palette (pink and yellow make orange) and paint it between them.
  • The brush is overloaded. Wipe it on a rag. Rinse before going into white.

Drying: About 10 minutes between steps (a hair dryer on low speeds it up). An hour after the last step before handling.

STEP 2 OF 19 · The night sky, 2 of 3

Circle in the moon

  1. Let the starry night sky dry to the touch first. A hair dryer on low speeds it up.
  2. Rinse the brush fully first: this is the lightest paint yet.
  3. Inside the outlined area. Its top is about 1/2 in from the top edge, and its left side is about 1/2 in from the left edge; it's about 2 in wide and 2 in tall.
  4. Paints, darkest first: Moon yellow, then Moon cream. The paint map shows where each goes.
  5. Brush: #10 round.
  6. Small circles with the tip of the brush make a bumpy edge. Around a bright spot, circular strokes move outward from it.
  7. It should leave a bumpy, soft edge.
  8. Moon yellow is much lighter than what it goes over: expect two or three thin coats, letting each dry.
  9. Watch out: The edge is too hard. Fix: soften it with lighter passes. Smudging with a finger works too.

Tip: The moon is the cool light, so it sits near the top left corner of the canvas: its top is about 1/2 in from the top edge and its left side about 1/2 in from the left edge. Keep it round, about 2 in tall. Swirl the Moon yellow in first, then circle Moon cream around it, leaving the gaps the after picture shows.

Basics: Let each layer dry

Let each layer dry

Not checked yet

  • Between steps, the paint underneath should be dry to the touch. A hair dryer on low speeds it up.
  • Painting into half-dry paint drags it up and turns it gooey and muddy.
  • Thick paint can feel dry on top and still be wet inside. Give thick areas longer.
  • Fine lines and light colors over dark especially need a dry layer underneath.
Basics: Light colors over dark need more than one coat

Light colors over dark need more than one coat

Not checked yet

  • One coat of white or a light color over a dark one usually looks gray and patchy.
  • Expect two or three thin coats, letting each dry. Use the paint thick, with little water.

STEP 3 OF 19 · The night sky, 3 of 3

Dot in the stars

  1. Let the starry night sky dry to the touch first. A hair dryer on low speeds it up.
  2. Rinse the brush well first. Dirty water tints every color with the last one.
  3. Inside the outlined area. Its top is about 1/2 in from the top edge, and its left side is about 1/2 in from the left edge; it's about 2 in wide and 2 in tall.
  4. Paint: Snow white.
  5. Mix enough Snow white for this step and step 19; cover it between them.
  6. Brush: #2 round. Load: Thick paint. Dip in fresh paint for each dot or small group.
  7. It should leave round, slightly raised dots, and a moon with no gaps on its right side.
  8. Leave what step 2 painted showing around these marks, as in the Result picture.
  9. Snow white is much lighter than what it goes over: expect two or three thin coats, letting each dry.
  10. Watch out: Uneven dots. Dipping into paint that has skinned over. Fix: keep a fresh puddle.
  11. Step back, squint, or take a photo to see it whole, and compare the big shapes with the picture.

Tip: Most of the white goes on the right side of the moon, filling the gaps left there, so the moon reads round and smooth. Then dot the stars across the sky where the after picture has them, small and spread out, none touching the moon.

The far pines 1 step

STEP 4 OF 19 · The far pines, 1 of 1

Stamp the dark pines

  1. Let the night sky dry to the touch first. A hair dryer on low speeds it up.
  2. Rinse the brush well first. Dirty water tints every color with the last one.
  3. Inside the outlined area, all the way across. Its top is about 2 in from the top edge and its bottom is about 5 in from the bottom edge.
  4. The outline also runs under where the snowy hill and drifts, and the lamplight on the snow will go: paint straight through there.
  5. The outline also reaches onto the starry night sky, painted already: there, only soften this paint into its edge and leave it showing.
  6. Paint: Pine navy.
  7. Brush: #6 fan. Load: Thin paint. Stroke the brush on the palette until the bristles fan out.
  8. Stamp only the tips, using the middle of the fan, not the side bristles. Start each tree at its point and zigzag down, pressing harder as the branches widen.
  9. Short strokes in different directions make a rough texture.
  10. It should leave clusters of fine, needle-like marks, light at each tree's tip and heavier toward its base, where the trees run together into a dark band.
  11. Watch out: A heavy, solid top. Too much pressure or paint at the start of the tree. Fix: add fine branches with a small round instead of more fan marks.
  12. Step back, squint, or take a photo to see it whole, and compare the big shapes with the picture.

Tip: Most of the pines go on the left side: the biggest group's left side is at the left edge, about 8 1/4 in wide, its top about 2 in from the top edge. A smaller group's left side is about 12 3/4 in from the left edge, about 3 1/4 in wide. Leave plain sky showing between the groups, and tap each tree from its pointed tip down, wider as you go.

Brushes

#6 fan
Stroke: Fan brush tapping how to do it, not checked yet

Fan brush tapping

Not checked yet

With. fan

Load. Thin paint. Stroke the brush on the palette until the bristles fan out.

Motion. Stamp only the tips, using the middle of the fan, not the side bristles. For a shape that widens, work from the top down in a zigzag and press harder as you go down. Short strokes in different directions make a rough texture.

What it leaves. Clusters of fine, needle-like marks, light at the top and heavier where pressed.

Then. If the top is too heavy, add a few fine lines with a small round instead of more fan marks.

Good for. a pine, from the top down in a zigzag, grass, with short strokes in different directions

Tap, then zigzag down

Dashed outline: what to paint in that picture. Arrows: which way to move the brush.

If it goes wrong.

  • Heavy, clumpy marks. The paint is too thick, the bristles are clumped, or you stamped with the side. Thin the paint a little, spread the fan, and stamp with the middle tips.

Try it on scrap paper first.

Drying: About 10 minutes between steps (a hair dryer on low speeds it up). An hour after the last step before handling.

The snow 2 steps

STEP 5 OF 19 · The snow, 1 of 2

Lay in the snow in shadow blue

  1. Let the far pines and the night sky dry to the touch first. A hair dryer on low speeds it up.
  2. Rinse the brush well first. Dirty water tints every color with the last one.
  3. Optional: lightly chalk its outline first, from the transfer outline in Before you start, measuring from the canvas edges with a ruler.
  4. Inside the outlined area, all the way across to the bottom edge. Its top is about 4 1/2 in from the top edge.
  5. Paint: Snow shadow blue.
  6. Mix enough Snow shadow blue for this step and step 16; cover it between them.
  7. Brush: 1 inch flat.
  8. Cut in the rolling top edge first with the brush's edge, then fill down with long sideways strokes that follow the roll of the hill.
  9. It should leave an even, solid blue field with a softly rolling top edge, as the after picture shows.
  10. Snow shadow blue is much lighter than what it goes over: expect two or three thin coats, letting each dry.

Tip: Cut in the top edge first: its top is about 4 3/4 in from the top edge, rolling as the after picture shows. Paint straight across the lower parts of the dark pines on the far hill.

Stroke: Curved strokes how to do it, not checked yet

Curved strokes

Not checked yet

Motion. Bend every stroke with the shape: from the top of each bump down along its curve, and around a round shape.

What it leaves. Marks that bend with the shape, which is what makes it look round or sloped.

Then. Use the darker mix along the shadow side and the lighter one along the lit side, both following the curve.

Good for. hills, pumpkin ribs, a balloon

STEP 6 OF 19 · The snow, 2 of 2

Shade the hollows between drifts

  1. Let the snowy hill and drifts, and the far pines dry to the touch first. A hair dryer on low speeds it up.
  2. Inside the outlined area, all the way across. Its top is about 5 in from the top edge and its bottom is about 1 1/2 in from the bottom edge.
  3. The outline also runs under where the white snow tops and the lamplight on the snow will go: paint straight through there.
  4. The outline also reaches onto the snowy hill and drifts, and the dark pines on the far hill, painted already: there, only soften this paint into their edge and leave them showing.
  5. Paint: Hollow blue.
  6. Brush: 3/4 inch flat. Load: Wiped nearly dry. Only the tip goes in the paint, and no water on the brush. It should feel dry and hard to apply.
  7. Light pressure, skimming the surface.
  8. It should leave feathery, broken, see-through marks that catch the canvas texture. Never a solid area.
  9. Watch out: It went on solid. The brush was too loaded. Fix: let it dry, then dry-brush the base color back over part of it.
  10. Step back, squint, or take a photo to see it whole, and compare the big shapes with the picture.

Tip: Skim sideways along the curve of each dip, all the way across, right over the snowy hill and drifts. Keep the darkest streaks low in each dip, leaving lighter blue on the drift tops, as the after picture shows.

The post and rails 3 steps

STEP 7 OF 19 · The post and rails, 1 of 3

Block in the post, arm and rails

  1. Let the snow and the far pines dry to the touch first. A hair dryer on low speeds it up.
  2. Rinse the brush well first. Dirty water tints every color with the last one.
  3. Optional: lightly chalk its outline first, from the transfer outline in Before you start, measuring from the canvas edges with a ruler.
  4. Inside the outlined area. Its bottom is about 1 1/4 in from the bottom edge, and its right side is at the right edge; it's about 6 in wide and 9 in tall.
  5. Paint: Wood brown.
  6. Brush: 1/2 inch flat.
  7. Start with the post as one tall rectangle. Then add the arm, the brace and the two rails as straight pieces, stroking along each one.
  8. It should leave one flat, even brown shape, with no shading yet, as the after picture shows.

Tip: Paint the tall post first, with up-and-down strokes. Then pull the arm out to the left of the post near its top, the slanted brace under it, and the two rails across to the right edge.

Stroke: Building from pieces how to do it, not checked yet

Building from pieces

Not checked yet

Motion. Start with one simple shape (an oval, a circle, or a rectangle). Then add the rest in curved pieces on each side, like ( ), smaller toward the edges.

What it leaves. A shape made of distinct curved segments with small gaps or overlaps between them.

Then. Soften where the pieces meet only if the shape should look smooth; otherwise leave the pieces showing.

Good for. shaped objects (a pumpkin is a center oval, then curved pieces on each side like ( ))

STEP 8 OF 19 · The post and rails, 2 of 3

Shade the dark side of the wood

  1. Let the wooden post, its arm and the fence rails, and the snow dry to the touch first. A hair dryer on low speeds it up.
  2. Inside the outlined area. Its bottom is about 1 1/4 in from the bottom edge, and its right side is at the right edge; it's about 5 1/2 in wide and 9 in tall.
  3. Paint: Dark wood.
  4. Brush: 1/2 inch flat. Load: Wiped nearly dry. Only the tip goes in the paint, and no water on the brush. It should feel dry and hard to apply.
  5. Light pressure, skimming the surface.
  6. It should leave feathery, broken, see-through marks that catch the canvas texture. Never a solid area.
  7. Watch out: It went on solid. The brush was too loaded. Fix: let it dry, then dry-brush the base color back over part of it.

Tip: The lantern will hang left of the post, so the shadow goes on the right side of the post. Stroke up and down the post and along the arm and rails. Keep the post's left side plain.

STEP 10 OF 19 · The lantern, 1 of 6

Block in the lantern glass

  1. Let the snow and the night sky dry to the touch first. A hair dryer on low speeds it up.
  2. Optional: lightly chalk its outline first, from the transfer outline in Before you start, measuring from the canvas edges with a ruler.
  3. Inside the outlined area. Its bottom is about 4 in from the bottom edge, and its right side is about 5 in from the right edge; it's about 3 in wide and 3 1/2 in tall.

  6. Brush: #10 round.
  7. Start with a rectangle for the middle of the glass. Then add the bulging sides in curved pieces, like ( ), narrowing toward the top and bottom.
  8. It should leave one flat, solid orange shape with clean edges, as in the after picture.
  9. Glow orange is much lighter than what it goes over: expect two or three thin coats, letting each dry.

Tip: The glass is a pot shape: a flat top, sides that bulge out, and a narrower flat bottom, about 3 in wide. It hangs below and left of the wooden post, its arm and the fence rails, with its top reaching into the sky.

STEP 14 OF 19 · The lantern, 5 of 6

Line the bars, ring and hook

  1. Let the glow and the brass cap and base, and the glowing lantern dry to the touch first. A hair dryer on low speeds it up.
  2. Inside the outlined area. Its top is about 2 in from the top edge, and its right side is about 5 1/2 in from the right edge; it's about 1 3/4 in wide and 5 in tall.
  3. The outline also runs under where the white snow tops and the lamplight on the snow will go: paint straight through there.
  4. The outline also reaches onto the glow and the brass cap and base, and the shadows in the snow, painted already: there, only soften this paint into their edge and leave them showing.
  5. Paint: Brass gold.
  6. Brush: #2 liner. Load: Thin paint. Swirl the brush in water, then in the paint. Add water if the line skips. Reload often.
  7. Hold the brush upright, with light, steady pressure. Pull each bar in one smooth stroke, bending with the glass. Keep the metal lines clean, not forked or wobbly.
  8. It should leave thin, flowing lines.
  9. Watch out: Skippy, broken lines. The paint is too thick. Fix: add water.

Tip: Start where the hook touches the arm of the wooden post: curl it up and over, then down into a ring above the cap, as the after picture shows. Then pull four bars from the cap down to the base, bowing with the glass. Go over the hook twice so it's thicker than the bars.

STEP 16 OF 19 · The snow on the fence, 1 of 1

Lay in the snow caps and front drift

  1. Let the lantern, post and rails dry to the touch first. A hair dryer on low speeds it up.
  2. Rinse the brush well first. Dirty water tints every color with the last one.
  3. Inside the outlined area. Its top is about 1 in from the top edge, and its right side is at the right edge; it's about 5 in wide and 10 in tall.
  4. Paint: Snow shadow blue.
  5. Brush: 1/2 inch flat.
  6. Bend every stroke with the snow: across the top of each cap in a low dome, and along the curve of the drift at the foot of the post.
  7. It should leave marks that bend with the shape, which is what makes it look round or sloped.
  8. Step back, squint, or take a photo to see it whole, and compare the big shapes with the picture.

Tip: Make each cap a soft mound that sits on the wood and hangs a little over its edges, as the after picture shows; the arm's cap is only a thin strip. Curve each stroke over the top of the mound. Leave the caps plain blue, with no white tops yet.

How Claude read your photosubject, light, layers

Before starting

Subject: A brass lantern glowing orange, hanging from a curled hook on a snow-capped wooden post with a rail fence, over rolling blue snow at night, with dark pines, a full moon, and stars.

Found in the image: just the picture

Done: none

Why: No bars, borders, captions, or frame: the whole image is the painting.

A night scene built around one warm light: a glowing brass lantern hanging from a snow-capped wooden post, a pool of lamplight on blue snow, dark pines, a full moon and stars. The lesson is about painting a deep night sky, flat blue snow, a wooden post from simple bars, and a glow built from orange to a pale core. The hard part is the lantern's shapes and keeping the warm glow clean against the blues.

Subject: A glowing brass lantern hanging from a snowy wooden post on a moonlit winter night, with dark pines and rolling snow behind
Focal point: The lantern's bright yellow core and the warm pool of light it throws on the snow below it
Light: Two lights: a cool full moon at the upper left, and the warm lantern in the middle, which lights the snow under it, the left side of the post, and the inside edges of its own brass frame. Snow tops catch the light on their upper edges.

What it saw, back to front

  1. The starry night sky
  2. The dark pines on the far hill
  3. The snowy hill and drifts
  4. The wooden post, its arm and the fence rails
  5. The glowing lantern
  6. The snow on the post, rails and drift
Why this techniquePaint along, back to front

Chosen by Claude: no --technique was given, and only this technique has version 2 keys.

ChosenPaint along, back to frontStart on a plain white canvas. Paint the sky first, then each part of the scene from farthest to nearest, each straight over the one behind it. Then the main subject, texture with simple brush moves, shadows, and highlights last.

Only acrylic-paint-along-beginner has version 2 keys, and it fits: a night sky first, far pines, snow fields, then the post, fence, and lantern in front, with the glow and highlights last.

Passed onBlock in, then build up (acrylic-block-in-beginner)

It has no version 2 keys (no v2_step_range or v2_rules), so the pipeline can't plan with it; the owner also prefers paint-along for acrylic beginners.

How the paint recipes were worked out17 paints, free

Paint doesn't mix like light on a screen: blue and yellow make green, not gray. So the recipes come from a pigment mixing model (Mixbox), not a guess. For each paint it tried every simple recipe from your tubes, up to three colors plus white, and kept the one that lands closest to the color in the painting. Delta E is how far off it lands: under 2 is hard to see, under 5 is close, and over 8 means these tubes can't quite make it.

Why the steps go in this order19 steps

Back to front, as the technique teaches: the sky to the bottom edge, the moon and stars, the far pines, the snow over the lower sky, the post and rails, then the lantern from its glass outward (glow, cap and base, bars and hook, shine), the snow on the fence, the lamplight on the snow, and the white snow tops last.

  1. 1. Blend the night sky

    The farthest thing, blended wet and run to the bottom edge so everything else can go over it.

  2. 2. Circle in the moon

    The moon sits on the sky, so it goes on as soon as the sky is dry.

  3. 3. Dot in the stars

    The stars are small dots on the dry sky, done before anything is in front of them.

  4. 4. Stamp the dark pines

    The far pines are the next layer back to front, dark silhouettes against the stars.

  5. 5. Lay in the snow in shadow blue

    The snow goes over the lower sky and the pines' feet, a flat blue field.

  6. 6. Shade the hollows between drifts

    Darker streaks in the dips give the snow its rolling shape before anything stands on it.

  7. 7. Block in the post, arm and rails

    The post and rails stand in front of the snow, so they're blocked in now from simple bars.

  8. 8. Shade the dark side of the wood

    The shadow side of the wood, away from the lantern, makes the post look round.

  9. 9. Light the side facing the lantern

    Tan streaks on the lantern side give the wood its light and grain.

  10. 10. Block in the lantern glass

    The lantern hangs in front of the snow; its glass goes on first as one flat orange bell.

  11. 11. Glow the middle of the glass

    Gold inside the glass starts the glow, each layer covering less than the last.

  12. 12. Light the core

    A small pale core is the brightest part of the glow.

  13. 13. Build the brass cap and base

    The brass cap and base frame the glowing glass once it's dry.

  14. 14. Line the bars, ring and hook

    The bars, ring and hook are thin lines over the dry glass and up to the arm.

  15. 15. Shine the brass edges

    Small pale shines on the brass edges facing the viewer finish the lantern.

  16. 16. Lay in the snow caps and front drift

    The snow on the post, arm and rails and the drift at the post's foot go over the dry wood.

  17. 17. Scumble the warm light on the snow

    The lamplight on the snow comes after the lantern so it reads as light from it.

  18. 18. Brighten the middle of the glow

    A lighter peach widens the pool and softens it into the snow.

  19. 19. Dry-brush the white snow tops

    The last step is the brightest highlights: white along every snow top.

Where Claude drew diagrams4 steps, free

Read every step as a first-time painter. The post and rails, the lantern's glass, its cap and base, and the bars and hook are shaped objects that appear whole in one step, so each gets a diagram. The rest are fills, blends, or repeated marks.

  • Step 7: Block in the post, arm and rails beginner check

    Noticed: The post, arm, brace and two rails appear at once and where they join isn't obvious.

    Pieces: The tall post first, then the arm and its diagonal brace, then two rails to the right edge.

  • Step 10: Block in the lantern glass beginner check

    Noticed: The glass is a bell shape a beginner would paint as a plain oval or a box.

    Pieces: A wide oval, then the top and bottom flattened into a bell.

  • Step 13: Build the brass cap and base beginner check

    Noticed: The cap's dome and brim and the flared base are two separate shapes on the glass.

    Pieces: A dome with a brim on top, then a flared band under the glass.

  • Step 14: Line the bars, ring and hook beginner check

    Noticed: The bars follow the glass's curve, and the ring and curled hook connect it to the arm.

    Pieces: Four bars curving with the glass, then the ring on top and the hook up to the arm.

What Claude would do differentlyfor the next lesson
  • Run on pipeline v3 from the owner's session for #237: the tools here, each helper an Opus subagent in a fresh context.
  • Plan writer (1 subagent): given plan-brief.md, the lesson folder, 00_canvas_frame.png and the technique file. Wrote 20 steps in 8 stages, 13 units, 12 renders, 7 mixes. Asked again for check's problems: a brush name the tools don't know and a merge of Pale snow blue into Snow shadow blue (it also dropped the step that merge left empty, so 19 steps), which re-rendered the chain from unit 4.
  • The plan writer was then asked to stop a drafted line naming Brass shine; it reworded two after lines, which changed two units' requests. erase was refused at the lesson's cost cap (/bin/bash.67 of /bin/bash.74), so the writer put both lines back exactly, and the actual cause, the unit name 'The bars, hook and brass shine' showing in a drafted Where line, was fixed by renaming the unit, which isn't in any request. Lesson: a unit name in a drafted line can trip check's paint test, and an after line's wording is part of the chain's requests.
  • Chain checker (1 subagent): marked U01 left (the stars stayed when the moon and stars were erased). The redo was refused at the cost cap, so it stays as a known problem.
  • Stage writers (8 subagents): given only their words/stage-NN folder. Round 1: 109 claims, 8 failed, 5 stages sent back once.

Known problems

Where the pictures aren't quite right. Paint it the way the step says and use the picture as a guide.

  • Step 2, Circle in the moon: The stars are already in the sky from the first step: the image model took the moon off but left every star, so the star step's pictures don't show stars being added (that step's picture changes the moon instead).
  • Step 3, Dot in the stars: Snow white was fitted to a dusty violet-gray (#aa93b9), far from the white its name says.
  • Step 11, Glow the middle of the glass: The step's after picture puts the gold as a ring just inside the glass's edge with orange left in the middle, and a small gold scrap in the sky above the glass, which the cap covers two steps later.
  • Step 12, Light the core: Glow cream was fitted to a warm yellow (#fce287), more yellow than the pale cream its name says.
  • Step 17, Scumble the warm light on the snow: The plan's touch of orange on the left of the front drift isn't in the step's picture, so the words leave it out.
